claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Low temperatures and high strain rates favor deformation twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Enhanced twinning sustains ductility while maintaining strength in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Homogenized, solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn can be treated as a single-phase solid solution structurally similar to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Temperature and strain rate should be varied in mechanical tests to probe the proposed transition.
Twin-boundary density and dislocation density provide measurable indicators of the relative activation of twinning and slip.
Co-free FeNiCrMn has sufficiently low stacking-fault energy to promote deformation twinning.
Dislocation glide becomes increasingly restricted at low temperature and high strain rate in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, thermal activation increases dislocation mobility and produces predominantly slip-based deformation.
High-rate, low-temperature deformation of FeNiCrMn should produce a measurable increase in deformation-twin density.
The high-rate, low-temperature regime should combine high strength with retained ductility.
Higher-temperature or lower-rate deformation of FeNiCrMn should revert to slip-dominated behavior.
In CoCrFeMnNi, slip and deformation twinning operate from 25 °C to 600 °C, whereas slip and partial recrystallization operate above 700 °C.
In analogous CoCrFeMnNi deformation, twinning is promoted by higher deformation rates.
The proposed mechanism applies to homogenized FeNiCrMn with minimal precipitation and phase segregation.
Significant secondary phases, severe residual stresses, or non-equilibrium microstructures may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in twin density in the high-rate, low-temperature regime would falsify the proposed slip-to-twinning transition.
Failure of mechanical performance to correlate with the expected microstructural transition would falsify the hypothesis.
